name: Sahel jihadist insurgency (Mali, Burkina Faso, Niger)
started: 2025-09-03 (JNIM fuel-blockade phase; the wider insurgency dates to 2012)
summary: Al-Qaeda's JNIM and the rival Islamic State Sahel Province are fighting the military juntas of Mali, Burkina Faso and Niger, which lean on Russia's Africa Corps and Turkish-made drones. Since September 2025 JNIM has waged economic siege warfare, choking fuel into Bamako, and in April 2026 it joined Tuareg rebels in the biggest offensive of the war, killing Mali's defence minister. The Sahel was Africa's deadliest militant Islamist theatre in 2025 with 9,826 deaths (Africa Center).

sides.name: Alliance of Sahel States (AES) juntas and Russia
members: Burkina Faso army and Volunteers for the Defence of the Homeland (VDP)
Niger Armed Forces and Domol Leydi volunteer self-defence groups (from March 2026)
Dozo hunter militias and Dan Na Ambassagou (central Mali)
backers: Russia: Africa Corps (ground troops, helicopters, convoy escort, air strikes)
Turkey (armed drones operated by the juntas; Akinci reported at Sevare, drones at Niamey airport)
Algeria (four Su-30 jets sent to Niamey after the Aug 2026 coup attempt)
leaders: Assimi Goita (Mali president, defence minister since 4 May 2026)
Gen. Daouda Traore (AES unified force commander)
Andrey Averyanov (Russian general overseeing Africa Corps)
sides.strength: Africa Corps in Mali estimated at 2,500-3,500 (Critical Threats, Apr 2026); Wikipedia cites about 1,000 (Dec 2024) to about 2,000 Russians after Wagner left (June 2025). Africa Corps in Niger about 100-300. Burkina Faso aims to train 100,000 reservists by end 2026 (Wikipedia, 2026 in Burkina Faso).

sides.name: JNIM (al-Qaeda in the Sahel)
backers: Self-financed through ransoms, gold, road taxation and fuel trade
leaders: Abou Houzeifa al-Bambari (spokesman who announced the blockade)
sides.strength: Roughly 6,000 fighters and probably growing (Critical Threats, Apr 2026). Africa Corps claimed 10,000-12,000 JNIM and FLA fighters took part in the April 2026 offensive (unverified).

sides.name: Islamic State Sahel Province (ISSP)
members: ISSP fighters in Menaka (Mali), Tillaberi and Tahoua (Niger), and Burkina's Sahel region
Defectors from JNIM, including Est commander Sadou Samahouna (early 2026)
leaders: No current leader reliably named in sources found

background: The current war grew out of the 2012 Tuareg rebellion and jihadist takeover of northern Mali, then spread into central Mali, Burkina Faso and western Niger. Coups in 2021 (Mali), 2022 (Burkina Faso) and 2023 (Niger) brought juntas that expelled French forces, turned to Russia (first Wagner, then from June 2025 the state-run Africa Corps) and formed the Alliance of Sahel States. JNIM, an al-Qaeda coalition formed in 2017, is the strongest armed actor; ISSP is its bitter rival, and their clashes since 2019 have killed more than 2,100 people (ACLED via Reuters).

The two groups fight in different ways. JNIM embeds with rural communities, taxes and governs, negotiates local deals, and uses blockades and mass-casualty raids on bases. ISSP is more brutal toward civilians and concentrated in the Mali-Niger borderlands around Menaka and Tillaberi, which in 2025 was the deadliest region in the central Sahel (more than 1,200 fatalities, ACLED). Why it matters: the juntas promised to restore security and instead the violence has hit record levels, while the insurgency is pushing south toward the coastal states.
year: The year opened with JNIM's fuel blockade at its peak. After announcing it on 3 Sept 2025, JNIM burned more than 300 tankers on the Senegal, Cote d'Ivoire and Guinea corridors, forced Mali to close schools nationwide from 26 Oct to 9 Nov 2025, and prompted the US and about a dozen states to tell citizens to leave. Convoys of 1,200+ tankers got through under Malian and Russian escort from late October, and JNIM extended the blockade to Niger-bound trucks on 1 Nov. On 7 Nov 2025 JNIM hit the Soumpi base in Tombouctou region, claiming 48 soldiers killed, and attacked Chinese-run mines near Bamako. Mali imposed fuel rationing on 22 Jan 2026.

On 29 Jan 2026 ISSP stormed Niamey's airport and Air Base 101 with small arms, explosives and armed drones, its first known drone use in Niger. In Burkina Faso JNIM, after diverting fighters to the Mali blockade, launched a coordinated wave from mid-February (Titao base, an ambush near Fada N'Gourma that killed about 50 forest guards); ACLED's Heni Nsaibia counted over 130 dead. A senior JNIM commander in the Est, Sadou Samahouna, defected to ISSP. JNIM raided Benin (Kofouno, Pendjari) in early March and ISSP hit the drone base at Tahoua airport on 8 March.

The turning point came on 25 April 2026, when JNIM and the Tuareg FLA attacked Kati, Bamako's air base, Sevare, Mopti, Gao and Kidal at once, using suicide car bombs, armed drones and fighters in Malian uniforms. Defence Minister Sadio Camara was killed in Kati and the intelligence chief badly wounded. Malian and Russian forces negotiated withdrawals from Kidal, Tessit, Ber and Intahaka and abandoned Labbezanga to ISSP. JNIM then declared a full blockade of Bamako (28 April), and in May launched an offensive against Dozo militias in Mopti and Segou regions. In Niger, JNIM killed 67 at a military engineering camp at Garbougna (14 May), ISSP overran camps at In-Ates and Banibangou (17 June), JNIM attacked Niamey airport again (18 June, 13 killed), and on 30 June JNIM struck simultaneously across the Burkina-Niger border. An ambush near Doungourou on the Bankilare-Tera road on 17 July killed 16 soldiers officially, 47 according to RFI.

In August JNIM hit San, and Niger's junta survived a coup attempt on 29-30 Aug 2026 only with Africa Corps help. On 10 Sept JNIM overran the Dioura camp in central Mali, killing around 100 soldiers and five Africa Corps personnel and taking dozens prisoner. On 6 Oct a Malian and Russian convoy reoccupied Kidal after the FLA withdrew.
situation: As of late October 2026 the juntas hold the capitals, regional towns and main bases, and Mali has regained Kidal, but JNIM dominates much of rural central and southern Mali, northern and eastern Burkina Faso, and the roads around Bamako, where its declared blockade persists. ISSP holds sway in the Menaka-Tillaberi-Tahoua borderlands and competes violently with JNIM. Niger's junta is weakened by the August coup attempt and two attacks on Niamey airport, and Mali's by the loss of its defence minister and a string of base overruns (Dioura in September). The dry season, which favours large offensives, starts in November.
technical: JNIM blockade method: ambush escorted tanker convoys, burn trucks, set roadside 'tax' checkpoints, kidnap drivers, and coerce transport firms (Diarra Transport was forced to accept JNIM rules on gender segregation). More than 300 tankers destroyed; 50+ burned on the Kolondieba-Kadiana road on 17-21 Oct 2025 alone (Wikipedia, Mali fuel blockade).

Targeted corridors: Senegal road RN1 via Kayes (Kaniara-Lakamane), Sikasso-Zegoua, Niono-Segou, Neguela-Soribougou, Kolondieba-Kadiana. After April 2026 JNIM roadblocks were reported at Soribougou (west of Bamako), Narena (southwest) and Ouelessebougou (south).

25 April 2026 commando raids on Kati and Bamako's air base used suicide vehicle-borne IEDs, armed drones and attackers disguised in Malian uniforms; the targets were leadership (Defence Minister Camara killed, intelligence chief Modibo Kone wounded) and air assets (Critical Threats).

Critical Threats assessed most of Mali's air and drone fleet was concentrated at Sevare and the Bamako air base, both hit on 25 April; a source cited by CTP refers to Turkish Akinci combat drones at Sevare.

Africa Corps aviation losses in 2026: a Mi-35 shot down in Gao region in April (crew and mobile fire group killed), a Mi-24 shot down near Tabrichat on 5 July; Russian equipment convoyed from Lome port reached Bamako on 25 July 2026.

ISSP's 29 Jan 2026 Niamey airport raid: 30+ gunmen with small arms, explosives and armed drones; an ammunition depot destroyed and civilian aircraft hit; Niger said 20 attackers killed, 11 captured, 4 soldiers wounded. Kanuri-speaking fighters on video suggest ISWAP help (LWJ; ACLED).

Niger's airports are now a target set: Niamey (ISSP 29 Jan, JNIM 18 June) and the military drone base at Tahoua airport (8 March, motorcycle-borne attackers). Coup plotters in August reportedly seized Turkish drones at Niamey airport.

Typical base-raid pattern (Dioura, Garbougna, Doungourou, In-Ates): large motorcycle columns plus armed pickups, overrun in hours, loot vehicles and weapons, film prisoners for propaganda, withdraw before air response. Dioura (10 Sept 2026): 100+ soldiers killed, 80+ captured, vehicles and weapons displayed by JNIM.

JNIM economic targeting extends to foreign mining: attacks on Chinese-run sites near Bamako (7 Nov 2025) and at Koniko, Sikasso (27 Nov 2025, one Chinese killed, six abducted); Morila gold mine hostages (3 Jan 2026). A reported USD 50-70 million ransom was paid for two Emiratis (ACLED).

JNIM vs ISSP: ISSP killed 40+ JNIM fighters in Burkina's Sahel region on 9-10 Feb 2026; the JNIM Est commander Sadou Samahouna defected to ISSP near Boni, Niger (ACLED). JNIM and ISSP first fought each other inside Niger in April 2026 (Reuters).

Burkina Faso claims to control 74% of its territory and to have retaken 600 villages (Feb 2026); it claimed 400+ militants killed and 353 weapons seized repelling JNIM at Sebba, Solhan and Gayeri on 30 June 2026 (government claims).
Djibo, capital of Soum, has been under JNIM blockade since 2020; in 2025, 70% of JNIM attacks around Djibo hit multiple troop positions at once, up from 20% in 2024 (ACLED via CTP, in ACCORD).

Niger answered with volunteer militias ('Domol Leydi', 28 March 2026); Mali relies on Dozo militias, which JNIM targeted in a May 2026 offensive in Bandiagara, Bankass and Djenne cercles; about 12 Bankass villages handed weapons to JNIM.

Civilian harm by state forces: HRW attributes a 15 June 2026 airstrike at Kyrnia/Kimya near Hombori (8 civilians) to Africa Corps; HRW reported Africa Corps summarily killed nine civilians including four children in July 2026.
casualties: Africa Center (2025 calendar year): 9,826 militant Islamist-linked deaths in the Sahel, about 50% in Burkina Faso, over 29% in Mali and 17% in Niger; Niger's violent activity rose 51%. ACLED: Tillaberi had 1,200+ fatalities in 2025, the most of any central Sahel region; Burkina's conflict has killed more than 26,000 since 2015 (ACLED via AFP, May 2025). Incident-level 2026 figures: Kati 25 April, 23 killed (hospital source); Garbougna, 67 killed (14 May); Niamey airport 18 June, 11 soldiers and 2 civilians killed; Doungourou 17 July, 16 (official) or 47 (RFI) soldiers; Dioura 10 Sept, about 100 soldiers (RFI) plus 5 Africa Corps. Government and Russian claims of insurgent dead (Africa Corps: 1,000+ in April 2026) are unverified. No rolling Oct 2025-Oct 2026 total was found; deaths almost certainly exceeded 10,000 across the three countries but this is an inference from 2025 data and 2026 trends.
displaced: No current national IDP totals were retrieved for this file. Incident data: more than 2,500 displaced after JNIM's 3 Nov 2025 attack on Lere, Tombouctou region (ACLED). Djibo's population swelled from about 30,000 to 300,000 because of displacement under siege (The New Humanitarian, 2024, via ACCORD). Kouakourou's population fled after JNIM took it on 18 July 2026 (Wikipedia).

timeline.event: JNIM announces a fuel blockade targeting supplies to Bamako and other cities.
Mali closes schools nationwide until 9 Nov because of fuel shortages.
US tells its citizens to leave Mali immediately.
JNIM extends its blockade to trucks coming from Niger.
JNIM attacks the Soumpi army base (Tombouctou), claiming 48 soldiers killed; simultaneous attacks on Chinese-run mines near Bamako.
Mali, Burkina Faso and Niger launch a joint AES force under Gen. Daouda Traore.
ISSP assaults Niamey's airport and Air Base 101 with drones and gunmen.
JNIM attacks Titao base and ambushes forest guards near Fada N'Gourma during a coordinated Burkina offensive (130+ killed over 12-22 Feb).
Gunmen attack the military drone base at Tahoua airport, Niger.
Joint JNIM-FLA offensive across Mali; Defence Minister Sadio Camara killed in Kati; Kidal falls.
JNIM declares a full blockade of Bamako.
JNIM ambush at Garbougna military engineering camp, Tillaberi, kills 67.
JNIM attacks Niamey airport; 11 soldiers and 2 civilians killed per government.
JNIM coordinated attacks on Makalondi, Torodi, Diagourou (Niger) and Sebba, Solhan, Gayeri (Burkina Faso).
Ambush near Doungourou on the Bankilare-Tera road kills 16 (official) to 47 (RFI) Nigerien soldiers.
Coup attempt in Niamey put down with Africa Corps support.
JNIM overruns the Dioura camp in central Mali; about 100 soldiers killed.
Malian and Russian forces reoccupy Kidal after an FLA withdrawal.

outlook: Watch the November-May dry season for large JNIM offensives, possible retaliation for the loss of Kidal, and whether the Bamako blockade tightens again. Watch for renewed JNIM-ISSP fighting in Niger and Menaka, further attacks on airbases and drone assets, and the political stability of the Niamey and Bamako juntas after the 2026 coup attempt and the Camara assassination. Critical Threats assesses JNIM aims to shape a new Bamako authority rather than seize the whole country.

zones.name: Bamako blockade ring
zones.note: JNIM checkpoints at Soribougou, Narena and Ouelessebougou after the 28 Apr 2026 blockade declaration; Kati and the air base were hit on 25 April.

zones.name: Kayes-Senegal fuel corridor (RN1)
zones.note: Main import route from Dakar; repeated tanker ambushes including 29 Jan 2026 (15 killed) and a bus mine near Bamako on 1 Jun 2026.

zones.name: Sikasso-Bougouni-Kolondieba corridor
zones.note: Cote d'Ivoire and Guinea fuel routes; dozens of tankers burned Oct-Nov 2025; record violence in Sikasso region in Oct 2025 (ACLED).

zones.name: Central Mali (Mopti, Segou, Bandiagara, Djenne)
zones.note: Katiba Macina heartland; JNIM offensive against Dozo militias in May 2026; Dioura camp overrun 10 Sept 2026; Kouakourou fell in July.

zones.name: Menaka-Tillaberi-Tahoua ISSP zone
zones.note: ISSP stronghold straddling Mali and Niger; Labbezanga taken by ISSP 27 Apr 2026; In-Ates and Banibangou camps overrun June 2026.

zones.name: Tera-Bankilare (Niger)
zones.note: Tera department had the highest violence in Tillaberi in 2025; Doungourou ambush 17 July 2026.

zones.name: Makalondi-Torodi-Say (Niger, JNIM)
zones.note: JNIM front facing Niamey from the southwest; Torodi prefect killed 4 Jan 2026; Garbougna and Kirtachi attacks May 2026; Makalondi, Torodi, Diagourou hit 30 June 2026.

zones.name: Niamey and Air Base 101
zones.note: Airport and base hosting Africa Corps and the AES command; attacked 29 Jan and 18 Jun 2026; seized briefly by mutineers 29 Aug 2026.

zones.name: Soum and Djibo (Burkina Faso)
zones.note: JNIM blockade since 2020; mass-casualty raids in 2025; JNIM moves openly through Soum (CTP).

zones.name: Burkina Est and W-Arly-Pendjari forests
zones.note: JNIM safe haven and launch pad into Benin, Niger and Togo; gold and timber income; Feb 2026 ambush killed about 50 forest guards near Fada N'Gourma.

zones.name: Burkina north (Titao, Seguenega, Ouahigouya)
zones.note: Titao base attacked 15 Feb 2026; linked to JNIM's Malian command.

battles.name: Attack on Dioura army camp
battles.place: Dioura, Tenenkou cercle, Mopti region, Mali (coordinates approximate)
battles.outcome: JNIM overran and looted the camp, then withdrew; camp still abandoned a week later.
battles.forces: JNIM first wave on the base plus fighters arriving from the east on motorcycles and heavily armed vehicles.
battles.losses: At least 100 soldiers killed (RFI, multiple sources), 5 Africa Corps killed, 80+ captured; vehicles and large weapons stocks seized. JNIM losses unknown.
battles.significance: Among the deadliest single attacks on the Malian army; propaganda videos of captured soldiers undercut the junta after the April shocks.

sources.label: Dakaractu (RFI): Dioura toll rises to about 100 soldiers killed

battles.name: Niamey coup attempt
battles.place: Niamey (presidency, Air Base 101, state broadcaster), Niger
battles.outcome: Coup failed; Base 101 recaptured on 29 Aug with Russian support.
battles.forces: Mutineers reportedly seized the airport, Turkish drones there, state TV and radio; Africa Corps gave air and ground support to Tiani.
battles.losses: No official toll; some mutineers killed; several Russians reportedly captured during the attempt.
battles.significance: Revealed frontline anger over the Presidential Guard's privileges, and that Russia is now a regime-protection force in Niger; Algeria sent Su-30s afterwards.

battles.name: Doungourou ambush on the Bankilare-Tera road
battles.place: Near Doungourou, Tera department, Tillaberi region, Niger (coordinates approximate)
battles.outcome: Heavy army losses; attackers withdrew under air attack.
battles.forces: Army detachment with air support in the counterattack.
battles.losses: Official: 16 soldiers killed, 23 wounded; RFI: at least 47 killed including the detachment commander, 50+ wounded; government says 15 attackers killed.
battles.significance: Illustrates the gap between official and independent tolls in Niger's deadliest region.

sources.label: AllAfrica (RFI): Niger, many soldiers killed in attack in the west

battles.name: JNIM coordinated attacks across the Burkina-Niger border
battles.place: Sebba, Solhan, Gayeri (Burkina Faso) and Makalondi, Torodi, Diagourou (Niger); mapped at Sebba
sides: Burkina Faso and Niger armed forces
battles.outcome: Most attacks repelled; Diagourou not repelled.
battles.forces: Simultaneous JNIM assaults on six positions in two countries.
battles.losses: Burkina claimed 400+ militants killed, 250+ motorcycles and 353 weapons seized (government claim, ACLED-reported).
battles.significance: Shows cross-border command and control by JNIM on both sides of the frontier.

battles.name: JNIM attack on Niamey airport
battles.place: Diori Hamani International Airport and air base, Niamey, Niger
battles.outcome: Repelled after more than two hours of fighting.
battles.losses: 11 security personnel and 2 civilians killed, 22 attackers killed, about 20 arrested (government).
battles.significance: Second attack on the capital's airport in six months, this time by JNIM, a day after ISSP overran In-Ates and Banibangou: evidence the rivals are competing through spectacular attacks.

sources.label: TimesLive (Reuters): Al-Qaeda-linked militants claim attack on Niger airport that killed 13

battles.name: Garbougna military engineering camp attack
battles.place: Garbougna, Tillaberi region, Niger (coordinates approximate, placed near Kirtachi)
battles.forces: JNIM ambush and assault force; army engineer camp.
battles.losses: 67 killed including several civilians (Wikipedia, 2026 in Niger).
battles.significance: Part of JNIM's May offensive along the Niger River south of Niamey, alongside the overrun of a National Guard camp at Kirtachi (12+ soldiers killed, 7 captured).

battles.name: JNIM offensive against Dozo militias in central Mali
battles.place: Bandiagara, Bankass and Djenne cercles, Mopti region, Mali (centred on Bankass)
sides: Dozo militias and Dan Na Ambassagou
battles.outcome: JNIM gains; around 12 villages in Bankass cercle surrendered weapons to JNIM.
battles.forces: JNIM raiding groups; local Dozo self-defence militias.
battles.losses: 30+ killed in Korikori and Gomossogou (7 May); 40 in Kouroude and Dougara (8 May) (Wikipedia); at least one Dozo leader killed (ACLED).
battles.significance: JNIM used the post-April momentum to dismantle the junta's militia allies in the centre, a precondition for controlling the Bamako-Mopti axis.

battles.name: Kati and Bamako commando attacks (killing of Sadio Camara)
battles.place: Kati and Bamako-Senou air base, Koulikoro region, Mali
battles.outcome: Attackers repelled from Kati and Bamako by end of day, but Defence Minister Camara killed and air assets hit; JNIM declared a Bamako blockade three days later.
battles.forces: JNIM commandos with suicide VBIEDs, armed drones and fighters disguised in Malian uniforms; Malian forces with helicopters; Africa Corps.
battles.losses: Kati: 23 killed, 16 wounded (hospital source); Sadio Camara, his wife and two grandchildren killed; intelligence chief Modibo Kone wounded. Africa Corps claimed 300 attackers killed at Kati and 200 at Bamako (unverified).
battles.significance: The deadliest blow ever struck at a Malian regime's leadership; it exposed the junta's core and Russia's inability to protect it, and opened the way to the northern collapse.

sources.label: Critical Threats: Fall of northern Mali, JNIM-FLA offensive

battles.name: JNIM February offensive in Burkina Faso (Titao and Tandjari)
battles.place: Titao (Nord) and Tandjari near Fada N'Gourma (Est), Burkina Faso; mapped at Titao
sides: Burkina Faso army, VDP, forest guards
battles.outcome: JNIM claimed heavy losses inflicted; Titao base attacked.
battles.forces: Coordinated JNIM attacks, at least 10 claimed and 30+ recorded by ACLED across Est, Centre-Nord and Nord.
battles.losses: About 50 forest guards killed at Tandjari; about 10 civilians at Titao including seven Ghanaian traders; over 130 killed overall (ACLED's Nsaibia); 120+ soldiers, forest guards and VDP (ACLED).
battles.significance: Marked JNIM's return to large operations in Burkina after months focused on the Mali blockade.

sources.label: The Defense Post (AFP): Jihadist offensive in Burkina Faso

battles.name: ISSP assault on Niamey airport and Air Base 101
battles.place: Diori Hamani International Airport and Air Base 101, Niamey, Niger
battles.outcome: Attack repelled, but an ammunition depot destroyed and aircraft and air force infrastructure damaged.
battles.forces: 30+ gunmen with small arms, explosives and armed drones (ISSP's first drone use in Niger).
battles.losses: Niger: 20 attackers killed, 11 captured, 4 soldiers wounded (official).
battles.significance: First jihadist assault on the capital's airport; showed ISSP freedom of movement up to Niamey and possible ISWAP involvement.

sources.label: Long War Journal: Islamic State claims assault on airport in Niger's capital

battles.name: Attack on Soumpi army base
battles.place: Soumpi, Niafunke cercle, Tombouctou region, Mali (coordinates approximate)
battles.outcome: Attack repelled with drone strikes after heavy losses.
battles.forces: JNIM assault force (size unknown); FAMa garrison supported by drones.
battles.losses: JNIM claimed 48 soldiers killed and over 100 wounded (ACLED).
battles.significance: The single deadliest event of 2025 in Tombouctou region, and part of November 2025, the region's deadliest month in two years; it showed JNIM could hit the north while running the fuel blockade in the south.
